notes:
Let me try a search instead.I've written notes for all 14 verses, but they rest on fewer sources than you asked for. Partway through, the tools hit their usage limit: no full page could be opened, and I got 9 searches done. Everything below comes from the long extracts those searches returned. Mostly these are the Bible Hub and StudyLight pages that collect several older commentaries on one verse. A point marked "BibleHub 5-x" comes from that page, and I've named the commentator where the page shows it.

Because of that, two sections are thin:
- **Protestant traditions:** I found no clear tradition-against-tradition split. The real debates (why Esther waited, Mordecai's refusal, the scepter as a picture of Christ) cut across traditions. I give each commentator's tradition only where the page labels it.
- **Missing sources:** I couldn't reach the Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal and Lutheran sites, the modern-scholarship sites or the Orthodox site. I found nothing on prosperity or word-of-faith teaching, so that is left out.

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- "The third day" means the third day of the fast Esther had called. Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist) — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-1.html. Ellicott agrees and notes that "royal apparel" literally reads "royalty" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-1.htm
- Gill agrees about the fast. He adds that one Targum (an ancient Jewish Aramaic paraphrase) puts it during Passover. He says mourning clothes would have been unfit before the king, and points to the Greek addition (Esther 15:1). Only those who were called could enter the inner court, though Aben Ezra says the doorkeepers could not stop the queen. The king's throne faced the gate, so he could see who came in — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-1.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says she rightly used "every legitimate means" to win the favour of a man who was both her husband and her king — same page.
- Matthew Henry says she acted while her devotions were still fresh; a heart enlarged by communion with God is made bold — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-1.html
- Coffman cites a relief from Susa showing Darius I on his throne holding a sceptre five or six feet long — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-1.html
- Bible Hub's own verse notes link "the third day" to Jonah and to the resurrection. They read her royal robes as a picture of Christ interceding, and her boldness as an echo of Hebrews 4:16 — https://biblehub.com/esther/5-1.htm
- Guzik says this took courage, given the king's poor record with his queens — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-5/

**v. 2**
- Gill says the king's favour came from God, who holds kings' hearts in his hand. The king had not called her for over 30 days, and Vashti was put aside for less. The scepter meant her offence was pardoned. Touching it showed thanks and submission — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-2.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown cites Persian and Assyrian carvings of a simple gold wand. Holding it out meant the intrusion was forgiven and the visit welcome; touching its tip was the normal sign of reverence. Poole reads it the same way — same page.
- Coffman points to Proverbs 21:1, the king's heart in the Lord's hand — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/esther-5.html
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) says she probably also kissed the scepter, as tradition holds — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/esther-5.html. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that the Vulgate (the old Latin Bible) says "kissed" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/esther-5.html

**v. 3**
- "Half the kingdom" is a figure of speech: the king will grant even a very large request (Constable) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html. Gill calls it "hyperbolical and courtly" and says it means anything reasonable. Benson says nothing reasonable would be refused — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-3.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says granting requests in advance was common among Eastern kings. Citing Herodotus, it adds that on one day a year the king had to grant any request made by a guest at his table. It compares Herod in Mark 6:23 — same page.
- Benson says God often heads off his people's fears and goes beyond their hopes — same page.
- Matthew Henry contrasts the two kings: Esther came to a proud, domineering man, while we come to a God of love — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_005.cfm

**v. 4**
- Gill says she invited Haman partly to please the king, but chiefly so she could accuse him to his face in private — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-4.htm
- Benson says honouring the king's favourite would win more of the king's affection — same page.
- Barnes says she was afraid to make her real request too suddenly, and expected the king to come back to it — same page.
- Guzik calls this tact: first she would win the king's confidence, and she wanted Haman there so she could later expose him — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-5/
- Kretzmann says her consideration for the favourite made the king even more eager to serve her — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/esther-5.html

**v. 5**
- The sources only cover this verse within verses 1–8. Coffman uses this passage as the point where Esther puts her request off to a second banquet — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-8.html

**v. 6**
- Barnes says that after the food was cleared, Persian banquets went on with fruit and wine. During this "banquet of wine" the king repeated his offer — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-8.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the king ate alone, with guests in a hall next door, but they were allowed to join him for wine — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-10.htm

**v. 7**
- Keil and Delitzsch say she starts with "my petition and my request" and then breaks off. She did not think it the right moment — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-8.htm

**v. 8**
- Clarke says she could see she was winning the king, but she wasn't yet confident. Providence used the delay to make room for chapter 6 — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-8.html
- Gill gives two reasons for the delay: to deepen the king's affection, and to make him expect a weighty request — same page.
- Poole offers several possible reasons (shyness, policy) but says the main one was Providence, which took away her courage to speak for now — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-8.htm
- Preceptaustin notes the delay was providential. On the sleepless night in between, the king learns that Mordecai once saved his life (6:1–2) — https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_5-7_commentary

**v. 9**
- Barnes calls Mordecai's failure to stand a serious breach of Persian etiquette — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-9.htm
- Benson and Poole say it showed he did not fear Haman and trusted God to deliver his people. Poole adds that Haman had given up any claim to respect by his murderous plan — same page.
- Gill says Mordecai feared his standing might be taken as worship of Haman — same page.
- The Cambridge Bible says Mordecai's return to the gate suggests he had taken off his mourning clothes now that there was hope. It says "moved" is better translated "trembled" — same page.
- Matthew Henry says Haman was puffed up by the invitation — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-9.html

**v. 10**
- Poole says Haman could easily have killed Mordecai on the spot; God's providence made him, in effect, chain his own hands — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-10.htm
- Gill says Haman thought one man beneath his personal revenge, since the whole people would soon suffer — same page.
- On Zeresh: Ellicott says her name probably comes from an old Persian word for "gold", and a Targum makes her the daughter of Tatnai (Ezra 5:3). Barnes agrees on "gold" — same page.
- Brown says the Hebrew for "restrained" means he forced himself to stay quiet — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jbs/esther-5.html

**v. 11**
- Haman had ten sons (9:7–10). Keil, as quoted, says the Persian king sent yearly gifts to the man with the most sons — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-13.html. Constable says Persians valued many sons, citing Herodotus — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html
- The Homiletical Commentary lists Haman's "riches, children, position, honour" and says material goods could not fill his soul — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-13.html

**v. 12**
- Constable's source says a banquet with the queen was a rare honour, because Persian officials guarded their wives closely — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html
- Lange says the author presents this as the peak of Haman's honour, to make his fall more striking — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/esther/5.htm
- Matthew Henry says Haman thought the queen was charmed by his company — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_005.cfm

**v. 13**
- Keil and Delitzsch say the Hebrew means "this is not equal to me", that is, it does not satisfy him — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-13.htm
- Poole says the real cause of his rage, being refused worship, was something he was ashamed to say — same page.
- Matthew Henry calls the verse a comment on Proverbs 21:24. A small slight torments a proud man — same page.
- Constable and Coffman say lesser people blow slights up; better people overlook them — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/esther-5.html
- Guzik applies it this way: the longing for approval is met only by being accepted in Christ (Ephesians 1:6) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-5/
- Utley calls it a sound insight into what a root of bitterness does — https://bible.org/seriespage/esther-5
- The Homiletical Commentary says Haman unknowingly foretells his own doom — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-13.html

**v. 14**
- Fifty cubits is about 75 feet. Ellicott says the height was meant to draw attention and increase Haman's glory — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-14.htm
- Poole and Gill say it was to disgrace Mordecai and frighten others. Gill adds that it turned out to be "for himself". Geneva says it means the tallest that could be found. Benson says the advisers saw that Haman would gladly drop his plan to wait for the day set by the lots — same page.
- Matthew Henry says it stood before Haman's own door — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_005.cfm
- Constable suggests it may have stood on a hill or building — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html
- Preceptaustin says "ask the king" is the key line. After chapter 6, Haman could no longer get that permission — https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_5-7_commentary

## Where commentators differ (across traditions, not along tradition lines)

- **Why Esther delayed (vv. 4–8):**
  - *She was afraid or hesitating:* the Pulpit Commentary calls her "too timid, perhaps too wary" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/esther-5.html. Kretzmann (Lutheran) thinks she lacked courage or was unsure — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/esther-5.html
  - *It was a deliberate plan:* Constable, citing Bush, sees "a shrewd and deliberate plan" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html. Guzik calls it wisdom — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-5/
  - *God directed it:* Spurgeon, as quoted, says it was not the right time and God led her to wait. A writer quoted by preceptaustin thinks it wasn't fear but the Lord holding her back — https://www.preceptaustin.org/esther_5-7_commentary. Matthew Henry gives all three options — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_005.cfm
- **Mordecai's refusal to rise (v. 9):** Benson and Poole praise it as confidence in God. The Pulpit Commentary notes he first refused only to bow down, on religious grounds. A line on the same page (it sits between the Ellicott and Pulpit notes, so I can't tell whose it is) calls the earlier "honourable independence" now "indefensible rudeness" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-9.htm
- **The scepter as a picture of the gospel (v. 2):** Some read it that way. Brown says Jesus holds out a scepter of grace — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jbs/esther-5.html. Constable quotes a gospel application — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/esther-5.html. The Lutheran Starke reasons from the lesser to the greater: if a pagan king gives grace, how much more will the Lord — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/esther/5.htm. Others stick to the historical setting (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, Barnes, on the pages above).
- **Lutheran voices (Lange):** Lange's commentary quotes Brenz praising Esther's faith in God and love for his church. It sees her as the dependent, scattered church standing before worldly power — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lange/esther/5.htm

## Other views

- **"Gallows" or impaling stake (v. 14):**
  - Barnes (labelled Presbyterian) says hanging was not a Persian punishment; crucifixion or impaling was meant — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/esther/5-14.htm
  - Clarke says the Hebrew word means simply wood or a pole, and he believes impaling is meant — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-14.html
  - Guzik likens this hatred to the hatred that crucified Jesus — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/esther-5/
  - Coffman answers critics who call the height ridiculous: the advisers only proposed that height, much like the saying "hang him as high as heaven" — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/esther/5-14.html
- **Catholic (Greek additions, vv. 1–2):** Catholic Bibles include a longer Greek account of this scene. Esther faints at the king's angry look. God then changes his mood to gentleness, and he leaps up and holds her until she recovers. In the Latin he says, "I am your brother; do not fear" — https://www.newadvent.org/bible/est015.htm
  - Protestant commentators know this text: Matthew Henry retells it, calling it "apocryphal" — https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Est/Est_005.cfm. Coffman says nothing in it is unreasonable even though the Hebrew lacks it — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/esther-5.html
- **God not being named:** GotQuestions says the book is written so readers see "God's unseen hand" behind each twist; the king is only a bit player — https://www.gotquestions.org/Xerxes-in-the-Bible.html
